files.lesson.md: --- order: 9 unit: models10 node: AC9M10A05 n1 uses: [AC9M9A06 n2, AC9M10A04 n1] # a, h and k in a curve (Year 9); choosing a model assumes: [AC9M10A04 n3] # judging a model is taught in class until its lesson is built connection: ball-arc title: Make a conjecture summary: "A conjecture is a claim about every case in a family, such as 'if a is bigger, the ball lands sooner'. Change one number at a time to test it, include a case that might break it, and refine it when one case disagrees." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Three planets, one 20 m cliff, one ball dropped on each. The rule for the ball's height has one number that changes from planet to planet. How would you find out what that number does?" app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8435 url: http://127.0.0.1:8435/index.html readySelector: "#sl-a" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: cliff.yml#explain-pic, caption: "With a = 2, the ball's height is h = 20 − 2t². The ball reaches the ground when the curve meets the dashed line." } --- A ball is dropped from the top of a 20 m cliff. Its height after $t$ seconds is $h = 20 - at^2$, where $a$ says how strong gravity is on that planet. The cliff, the planets and every value of $a$ are made up for this lesson. ## Predict: which curve is the strong one ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to which curve belongs to the biggest a shows who reads the rule (a bigger a takes more off the height each second) and who guesses from the shape." check: type: predict q: "The three curves show a ball dropped on three planets, where $a$ is $1$, $2$ and $5$ in some order. Which curve is the planet with $a = 5$?" options: - "A, the one that lands last" - "B, the one that lands first" - "C, the middle one" - "They all land together, since the cliff is the same" actual: "B. Every second, the ball loses a × t² metres, so a bigger a takes height off faster and the ball lands sooner. A has the smallest a (1) and lands at about 4.5 s. C is a = 2 and lands at about 3.2 s. B is a = 5 and lands at 2 s." ``` The planets all drop the ball from the same height. Make a guess before you check. ## Run: change one number ```step stage: run insight: "Changing only a, one value at a time, and reading the landing time each time is how you collect cases for a conjecture." try: { playground: board, starter: "cliff.yml#run", height: 640 } check: { type: board, text: "Set $a$ to 1, then 2, then 4. Each time, read when the ball lands. Stop at $a = 4$. Then say in one sentence what happens to the landing time as $a$ goes up.", when: "a = 4" } ``` The graph draws the ball's height. The dashed line is the ground, and the board marks where the curve meets it. The table shows the height each second. ## Investigate: what makes a conjecture ```step stage: investigate insight: "A conjecture is an if-then claim about every case in a family. Cases that agree support it, they never prove it, and one case that disagrees rejects it." tasks: - check: type: question q: "Which of these is a conjecture about the ball's rule, a claim a new case could prove wrong?" options: ["If $a$ is bigger, then the ball lands sooner", "When $a = 2$, the ball lands at about 3.2 s", "The graph is a curve", "The cliff is 20 m high"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That is true, but it only says something about one value of a. A conjecture covers the whole family.", "That describes the picture. Nothing in it can be wrong for a new value of a.", "That's a fact the problem gives you, not a pattern you've noticed."] explain: "A conjecture says what happens for every $a$ in the family, so a value you haven't tried yet could show it wrong. 'If $a$ is bigger, then the ball lands sooner' does that." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#ivy" text: "Ivy tests her conjecture. Click the line where her reasoning goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: one-case-confirms explain: "Line 3: two tests that agree support the conjecture, but they don't prove it. A third value, one she hasn't tried, could still disagree." - check: type: question q: "Zara tests $a = 1, 2, 4$ and $5$. The ball lands sooner every time. What can she say?" options: ["The conjecture is supported, but one case that disagrees would still reject it", "The conjecture is proved, because four cases is plenty", "The conjecture is rejected, since she hasn't tried every value", "Nothing, because four cases is too few to say anything"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Four, or four hundred, agreeing cases still leave the next case untested.", "Not trying every value doesn't reject it. Only a case that disagrees does.", "Agreeing cases are evidence. They count as support, just not as proof."] explain: "Cases that agree make the conjecture more believable. Only a case that disagrees can reject it, and only a reason that covers every case can prove it." - check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "The claim: 'In $y = x^2 + c$, if $c$ is bigger, the curve crosses the $x$-axis in more places.' For $c = -4$ it crosses in 2 places. Test $c = 4$. In how many places does $y = x^2 + 4$ cross the $x$-axis?" steps: - ["$x^2 + 4 = 0$", "the curve crosses the axis where y is 0"] - ["$x^2 = -4$", "subtract 4 from both sides"] - ["no number squared is negative, so there are 0 places", "the curve stays above the axis"] - ["0 is fewer than 2, so the claim is rejected", "a bigger c gave fewer places"] answer: "0" answerLabel: "places it crosses" feedback: - ["2", "That's the c = -4 case. Put c = 4 in: x² + 4 = 0 has no solution."] criteria: - "I set y = 0 for c = 4." - "I said how many places it crosses." - "I said whether the claim is supported or rejected, and why." explain: "x² + 4 = 0 has no solution, because x² is never negative. The curve crosses in 0 places, fewer than the 2 at c = -4, so the claim is rejected." ``` ### What counts as a conjecture ### Find the mistake Read Ivy's working. Where does she go too far? ### Supported or proved ### Test one on paper Here's how to test a conjecture on a different family, $y = ax^2$. ```worked \text{Conjecture: if } a \text{ is bigger, the curve is narrower.} :: Write the claim as an if-then about the whole family, so a new value of a could show it wrong. a = 1,\; 2,\; 3 :: Try some positive values. At x = 1 the heights are 1, 2 and 3, and the curve is steeper each time. \text{Positive cases agree} :: These support the conjecture. They are not enough, so choose a case that might break it. a = -1 \text{ and } a = -3 :: Try negatives. Here -1 is bigger than -3. y = -1 \text{ and } y = -3 \text{ at } x = 1 :: The a = -3 curve is lower at x = 1, so it is the narrower one. \text{A bigger } a \text{ gave the wider curve} :: One case that disagrees rejects the conjecture as it is written. \text{If } a \text{ is further from } 0 \text{, the curve is narrower.} :: Refine it, then test it on new values. ``` Now try one on paper. The claim is: "In $y = x^2 + c$, if $c$ is bigger, the curve crosses the $x$-axis in more places." For $c = -4$ the curve crosses at $x = 2$ and $x = -2$, so two places. Test $c = 4$. How many places does it cross? ## Modify: look for the edge ```step stage: modify insight: "A good test is one that might break the conjecture: the edge of the family (a = 0, a below 0) and then a refined claim to try again." try: { playground: board, starter: "cliff.yml#vary", height: 640 } tasks: - hint: ["Try a = 0 first, then a = -1.", "Read the height at the start and after a few seconds."] check: type: question q: "Set $a$ to 0, then to $-1$. What does the ball do?" options: ["It never lands: at 0 it hangs at 20 m, and below 0 it climbs", "It lands at once, because a is 0", "It lands later than any other value of a", "It lands at the same time as a = 1"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "With a = 0 nothing takes height off, so it stays at 20 m.", "It has no landing time at all, so 'later than any other' doesn't fit.", "At a = 1 it lands at about 4.5 s. Read the board at a = 0."] explain: "At a = 0 the height stays 20 − 0 × t² = 20. For a below 0 the height grows. The ball never reaches the ground, so there's no landing time to compare." smaller: check: { type: number, q: "With $a = 0$, what is the ball's height after 3 seconds? Use $h = 20 - at^2$.", answer: 20, explain: "20 − 0 × 9 = 20. Nothing takes height off." } - hint: "Landing is when the height is 0: 20 = a × t × t." check: { type: number, q: "Zara refines it: 'If $a$ is bigger **and above 0**, the ball lands sooner.' Test it with a small value. For $a = 0.2$, when does the ball land? (Solve $20 - 0.2t^2 = 0$.)", answer: 10, feedback: [[100, "100 is t². Take the square root."]], explain: "0.2t² = 20, so t² = 100 and t = 10 s. That's later than 4.5 s at a = 1, which fits her refined claim." } - check: type: question q: "Read the landing time at $a = 1$ and at $a = 4$ on the board. Four times the $a$ gives a landing time that is..." options: ["Half as long", "A quarter as long", "Four times as long", "The same"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "A quarter of 4.5 s would be about 1.1 s. At a = 4 the board shows about 2.2 s.", "A bigger a lands sooner, so the time can't grow.", "It changes. Compare 4.5 s with the board's reading at a = 4."] explain: "At a = 1 the ball lands at about 4.5 s and at a = 4 about 2.2 s, which is half. That's a second pattern to turn into a conjecture and test." ``` ### Hanging forever ### A small value of a ### Four times as much ## Practise: conjectures ```step stage: practise insight: "Spotting a testable claim, testing it with numbers, finding the single case that rejects one, and (review) a quadratic equation." tasks: - check: type: question q: "Which of these is a conjecture you could test on $y = ax^2$?" options: ["If $a$ is positive, then the curve opens upward", "The curve $y = 3x^2$ passes through $(1, 3)$", "Graphs of curves are interesting", "When $a = 2$, $y = 8$ at $x = 2$"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That is a fact about one curve. A conjecture covers the whole family.", "That isn't a claim a new case could show wrong.", "That is one calculation, not a claim about every a."] explain: "It says what happens for every positive $a$, so a new value could show it wrong." smaller: check: { type: question, q: "'The curve $y = 3x^2$ passes through $(1, 3)$.' Is that about one value of $a$ or every value?", options: ["One value", "Every value"], answer: 0, explain: "It's about a = 3 only. A conjecture says something about every a in the family." } - check: type: number q: "A student's conjecture: 'In $y = ax^2$, doubling $a$ doubles $y$ at $x = 3$.' Test it. For $a = 2$, $y = 18$ at $x = 3$. What is $y$ at $x = 3$ for $a = 4$?" answer: 36 feedback: - [12, "That's 4 × 3. Square the 3 first: 4 × 9."] explain: "4 × 3² = 4 × 9 = 36, which is twice 18. This case agrees, so the conjecture is supported." - check: type: question q: "Which pair of values rejects the claim 'if $a$ is bigger, the curve $y = ax^2$ is narrower'?" options: ["$a = -1$ and $a = -3$", "$a = 1$ and $a = 2$", "$a = 2$ and $a = 5$", "$a = 0.5$ and $a = 1$"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "At a = 2 the curve is narrower than at a = 1, so this pair agrees.", "At a = 5 the curve is narrower than at a = 2, so this pair agrees.", "At a = 1 the curve is narrower than at a = 0.5, so this pair agrees."] explain: "-1 is bigger than -3, but the a = -3 curve is the narrower one. One case that disagrees rejects the claim." - check: type: number q: "Review: solve $x^2 + 4x = 0$. What is the negative solution?" answer: -4 explain: "x(x + 4) = 0, so x = 0 or x = -4." ``` ### Testable or not ### A test with numbers ### The case that breaks it ### Review From the last unit: a quadratic with a missing number term. ## Make: back to the cliff ```step stage: make insight: "Coming back to the three planets: use what the tests showed to find the a that makes the ball land at a chosen time, and say what the model leaves out." tasks: - hint: ["The ball lands when the height is 0, at t = 2.", "Put t = 2 into 20 − a × t² and set it equal to 0."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A planet needs the ball to land at exactly 2 seconds. Use $20 - at^2 = 0$ at $t = 2$ to work out $a$. Is that planet stronger or weaker than $a = 2$?" steps: - ["$20 - a \\times 2^2 = 0$", "the height is 0 at t = 2"] - ["$20 - 4a = 0$", "2² is 4"] - ["$a = 5$", "20 ÷ 4"] - ["5 is bigger than 2, so the planet is stronger", "a bigger a lands sooner, as the conjecture says"] answer: "5" answerLabel: "a" feedback: - ["10", "That's the time when a = 0.2. Here t is 2: put it in and solve for a."] - ["20", "That's the starting height. Put t = 2 into 20 − a t² and solve for a."] criteria: - "I put t = 2 into the rule and set the height to 0." - "I solved for a." - "I compared my a with 2 and said whether the planet is stronger or weaker." explain: "20 − 4a = 0 gives a = 5. That's bigger than 2, so the planet is stronger and the ball lands sooner, which fits the conjecture." - check: type: question q: "A class drops a real ball from a roof, films it and compares the landing time with the rule. It lands a little later than the rule says. What is the best response?" options: ["The rule is a model that leaves things out, such as air pushing back on the ball; say so and check how big the gap is", "The conjecture is proved wrong, so throw the rule away", "The film must be wrong, since the rule is maths", "The rule is proved right, since the times are close"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "A small gap doesn't mean the rule is useless. It means the rule leaves something out.", "Measurements can be a little off, but the rule is a simplified model, not the truth.", "Close doesn't prove a rule right. It supports it, as in the conjecture tests."] explain: "The rule leaves out air resistance, so a real ball falls a little more slowly. Saying what a model leaves out, and how much it matters, is part of testing it." ``` ### The planet that lands at 2 seconds Back to the cliff. Work it out on paper first, then type your answer. ### A real ball The cliff, the planets and every value of $a$ are made up, and the rule leaves out air pushing back on the ball. Your class could drop a ball from a measured height, film it and compare it with the rule. Sources: the 20 m cliff, the planets and every value of $a$ are made up for this lesson. **Also used in** - **Science investigations.** A fair test changes one variable at a time, and a hypothesis is a conjecture that results can support or reject. - **Design.** A designer tunes one setting at a time and tests it at the edges before trusting it. - **Next.** Judging a model, and generalising a pattern across several experiments. ```teacher summary: Students vary one number in a rule on a graphing board, state a conjecture as an if-then claim, test it on cases chosen to break it, and refine it when one case disagrees (AC9M10A05, node 1). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 10 min · Investigate 12 min · Modify 8 min · Practise and Make 15 min goals: - I can state a conjecture as a claim that could be wrong. - I can test it by changing one number at a time, including a case that might break it. - I can say whether the cases support it or reject it, and fix it if it fails. struggle: Choosing a test. Students pick more cases like the ones that already worked. Ask 'which value might break it?' and point at zero, negatives and very small numbers. before: > Do the Run board yourself first. The graph draws the height of a ball dropped from a 20 m cliff, h = 20 − at², and marks where it meets the ground. The dashed line is the ground. The slider is a, how strong gravity is on a made-up planet. The one idea: a conjecture is a claim about every case in a family ("if a is bigger, the ball lands sooner"), not a note about one graph. Cases that agree support it and can never prove it. One case that disagrees rejects it, and the useful next move is to refine the claim and test it again. Students have used a board to vary a and b in a line, and a, h and k in a curve (Year 9). Here the new move is writing the claim down first and then choosing tests, rather than playing with the slider. The conjecture holds for a above 0 and has no landing time at a = 0 (the ball hangs at 20 m) or below (it climbs). The worked example uses y = ax² for a conjecture that fails: with negative a, a bigger a gives a wider curve. Everything is made up: the cliff, the planets and the values of a. A class option: on Earth, a is a little under 5, so a = 5 is close to a real drop from 20 m (about 2 s). Let students look the number up for themselves if they ask; the lesson does not depend on it. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands before the Run. Those who pick the widest curve for the biggest a are guessing from the look of the curve. Don't correct it yet." - "Run: ask students to write the conjecture in the form 'If … then …' before they test anything." - "Investigate: the bug is Ivy calling two agreeing tests a proof. Ask how many tests would be enough." - "Paper: the try-one after the worked example and the Make question are worked on paper first." stuck: - see: A student writes an observation ('at a = 2 it lands at 3.2 s') and calls it a conjecture. ask: Could a new value of a make this wrong? fix: "A conjecture says what happens for every a in the family: 'If a is bigger, then …'." - see: A student tests only values near the ones that worked. ask: Which value of a might break it? fix: "Try the edge: zero, a negative, and a very small number." - see: A student says the conjecture is proved after two or three agreeing cases. ask: What would one case that disagrees do to it? fix: Agreeing cases support a conjecture. A proof says why it is true for every case (Year 10 proof lessons). stretch: "Landing time is the square root of 20 ÷ a. Test: is the landing time halved when a is quadrupled? Then find a rule for how it changes when a is multiplied by 9." support: A table with columns a, landing time and 'sooner or later than the row above'. Fill it from the board for a = 1, 2, 4 and 5, then say what the last column shows. leads: > Next: judging a model, and generalising a pattern across several experiments (10A05 n4, taught in class). Making and testing conjectures comes back whenever students use a graphing tool on a new family. Where it leads: the proof lessons in Angles (Some cases or every case?), where a conjecture that survives every test is finally argued for every case. exit: q: In y = ax², Mia says 'if a is bigger, the curve is narrower'. Write one test that could show her wrong, and say what you'd expect to see. a: "Any negative pair: a = −1 and a = −3. −1 is bigger, but y = −x² is wider than y = −3x². One case that disagrees rejects the claim; she could change it to 'if a is further from 0'." explain: > A **conjecture** is a claim about a whole family of cases that you can test: "If $a$ is bigger, then the ball lands sooner." - **State it as if-then**, so a new case could show it wrong. - **Test it** by changing one number at a time, and include a case that might break it (zero, a negative, a very small number). - **Cases that agree support it**; they don't prove it. **One case that disagrees rejects it**, and you can then refine the claim. sources: - title: "Made up for this lesson: the 20 m cliff, the planets and every value of a. The rule h = 20 − at² is a simple model of a dropped ball without air resistance." url: https://tutorials.learningwaypoints.com/maths/functions/make-a-conjecture/ checked: 2026-10-25 ```

# Boards for "Make a conjecture". A ball is dropped from a 20 m cliff on made-up planets; a is how strong gravity is
# (made up). The height after t seconds is h = 20 - a t^2. The dashed line is the ground; the board marks where they meet.

# region: run
widget: graph
x: -1, 6
y: -3, 22
grid: 1, 2
axes: t (seconds), h (metres)
slider a: 0.5, 6, 1, 0.5
plot: y = 20 - a x^2, from 0
plot: y = 0, dashed
cross: 1, 2
table: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
# endregion

# region: vary
widget: graph
x: -1, 6
y: -3, 22
grid: 1, 2
axes: t (seconds), h (metres)
slider a: -2, 6, 1, 1
plot: y = 20 - a x^2, from 0
plot: y = 0, dashed
cross: 1, 2
# endregion

# region: explain-pic
widget: graph
x: -1, 6
y: -3, 22
grid: 1, 2
axes: t (seconds), h (metres)
plot: y = 20 - 2 x^2, from 0
plot: y = 0, dashed
cross: 1, 2
# endregion

# Ivy's working for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: ivy
Conjecture: if a is bigger, the ball lands sooner.
Tests: a = 1 lands at about 4.5 s. a = 2 lands at about 3.2 s.
The landing time went down both times, so the conjecture is proved.
So it is true for every value of a.
# endregion
